title: Index Signatures
summary: An **index signature** like `{ [key: string]: T }` describes an object whose keys aren't known ahead of time — a dictionary mapping any string key to a value of type `T`. It's how you type maps, lookup tables, and dynamic property bags safely.

subtopics.title: String and number index signatures
subtopics.explanation: An index signature declares the type of values reachable by a key whose exact name you don't know: `[key: string]: number` means 'any string key maps to a number'. You can also use `[index: number]: T` for array-like numeric access. JavaScript object keys are strings, so a number index must be compatible with the string one if both exist.

subtopics.title: Dictionaries of unknown keys
subtopics.explanation: Index signatures shine for dictionaries/maps where keys are data, not fixed property names — word counts, id-to-entity lookups, feature flags. Any key access is allowed and typed as the value type, so you trade exhaustive key knowledge for flexibility.

subtopics.title: Record<K, V> vs index signatures
subtopics.explanation: `Record<K, V>` is a utility built on index/mapped types. With `K = string` it's equivalent to a string index signature, but Record can also restrict keys to a known union (`Record<'a' | 'b', number>`), which an index signature can't. Prefer Record for finite key sets and for concise, readable map types.

subtopics.title: Combining with known keys
subtopics.explanation: You can mix explicit properties with an index signature, but every named property's type must be assignable to the index signature's value type. This models objects with a few guaranteed fields plus arbitrary extras.
subtopics.example: interface Config { name: string; [key: string]: string; }

subtopics.title: noUncheckedIndexedAccess pitfall
subtopics.explanation: By default, indexing returns `T` even though the key may be missing — a lie that causes runtime undefined bugs. The `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` compiler flag makes index access return `T | undefined`, forcing you to handle the missing case. It's the safe-but-stricter default many teams enable.
subtopics.example: const v = counts['missing']; // T, but really undefined at runtime

subtopics.title: When to use index signatures
subtopics.explanation: Use an index signature when keys are open-ended and come from data. Use a fixed interface (or Record over a key union) when the set of keys is known. If you find yourself listing the same value type for many unknown keys, that's the signal for an index signature or Record.
subtopics.example: // open keys -> index signature/Record; known keys -> interface

foundations.overview: Index signatures let you type objects used as dictionaries — where keys are runtime data rather than a fixed, known set. Instead of naming every property, you declare the type of the key and the type of every value reachable by such a key, giving safety to lookup tables, caches, and dynamic property maps.
foundations.formalDefinition: An index signature [key: K]: V (where K is string, number, or symbol) declares that any property accessed by a key of type K has value type V. It constrains all members, including explicitly named ones, which must be assignable to V.
foundations.whyItMatters: Real apps are full of maps: id-to-entity caches, counts, config bags, i18n dictionaries. Index signatures are how you type them, and the noUncheckedIndexedAccess pitfall is a favourite interview topic that separates careful engineers from careless ones.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of an index signature as describing the shape of a dictionary: 'for any key of this type, the value is that type'. It types the door, not the individual rooms.
foundations.browserPerspective: Index signatures are erased at compile time. At runtime it's just a plain JavaScript object (or you might choose a Map). The compiler adds no key existence checks unless you enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Typing localization dictionaries ({ [key: string]: string }), feature-flag maps, normalized state (byId lookups), word/frequency counts, and HTTP header bags.
foundations.businessImpact: Correctly typed dictionaries prevent undefined-access crashes on dynamic keys, while strict index access stops 'works in dev, crashes in prod' lookup bugs.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Index signatures and Record give a uniform way to type dynamic data, reducing ad-hoc casts to any and making caches/lookups self-documenting.
foundations.performanceImpact: No runtime cost from the types. The runtime choice (object vs Map) matters more: Map handles non-string keys and large/changing key sets better than plain objects.
commonUseCases: Lookup tables / caches keyed by id

commonMisconceptions.myth: Indexing a dictionary always returns a defined value.
commonMisconceptions.reality: By default the type says T, but a missing key returns undefined at runtime. Enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess to surface this as T | undefined.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Record<K, V> and an index signature are completely different.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Record<string, V> is essentially an index signature; Record additionally supports restricting keys to a known union, which an index signature cannot.

debuggingLab.title: Trusting an index lookup that isn't there
debuggingLab.symptom: Reading a dictionary key that doesn't exist returns undefined at runtime, then calling a method on it throws 'Cannot read properties of undefined'.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Without noUncheckedIndexedAccess, prices[item] is typed number even for missing keys, so the compiler permits price.toFixed(2). At runtime prices['banana'] is undefined and toFixed throws. The default index typing hides the possibility of a missing key.
commonMistakes: Assuming an index lookup always returns a present value.
Leaving noUncheckedIndexedAccess off, so the compiler can't warn about missing keys.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Treat the lookup as possibly undefined (as noUncheckedIndexedAccess would) and guard before using it.

theory.question: What is an index signature and when should you use one?
theory.directAnswer: An index signature like [key: string]: T types an object whose keys aren't known in advance, declaring that any key of that type maps to a value of type T. Use it for dictionaries and maps — caches, counts, config bags — where keys come from runtime data. Use a fixed interface (or Record over a key union) instead when the set of keys is known.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A member declaration that types all properties reachable by a given key type rather than naming each one.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Objects are often used as dictionaries with dynamic keys; index signatures type that pattern without listing every key.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The signature constrains all members to the value type; accessing any key of the declared key type yields that value type (T, or T | undefined under strict index access).

theory.whyImportant: Dictionaries are everywhere in real apps, and choosing between index signatures, Record, and fixed interfaces is a common design question.
theory.realWorldExample: A normalized store's byId map is typed { [id: string]: Entity } so any id lookup returns an Entity (or undefined under strict access).

nestedTopics.title: Key types
nestedTopics.explanation: Keys can be string, number, or symbol; numeric keys must be compatible with a string index if both exist.

nestedTopics.title: Constraint on named members
nestedTopics.explanation: Any explicitly named property's type must be assignable to the index value type.

followUps.question: Can you mix named properties with an index signature?
followUps.answer: Yes, but each named property's type must be assignable to the index signature's value type.

followUps.question: Object with index signature or a Map?
followUps.answer: Use a Map for non-string keys, frequent insert/delete, or large dynamic key sets; an object/index signature is fine for simple string-keyed lookups.

theory.question: How does Record<K, V> differ from an index signature, and when would you pick each?
theory.directAnswer: Record<string, V> is essentially a string index signature, but Record can also restrict keys to a known union — Record<'a' | 'b', V> — which an index signature can't express. Use Record for finite key sets and for concise, readable map types; use a raw index signature when keys are truly open-ended and you want it inline in an interface (especially when combining with named properties).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Record<K, V> is a built-in mapped type producing an object with keys K and values V; an index signature is a member form on an interface/type.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Record offers a concise, composable map type including over key unions; index signatures integrate into a larger interface alongside named members.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: With K = string they're equivalent; with K = a union, Record requires every key in the union to be present, behaving like an exhaustive map rather than an open dictionary.

theory.whyImportant: Picking the right one shows judgment about whether keys are finite/known or open-ended.
theory.realWorldExample: Record<Status, Handler> guarantees a handler for every status; { [k: string]: Handler } allows any string key but no exhaustiveness.

nestedTopics.title: Exhaustiveness
nestedTopics.explanation: Record over a union requires all keys, helping catch a missing case.

nestedTopics.title: Composability
nestedTopics.explanation: Record reads cleanly and composes with other utility types.

followUps.question: Does Record over a union guarantee keys exist at runtime?
followUps.answer: No — it's compile-time only. The type requires you to provide all keys in your object literal, but it can't verify a value built dynamically actually has them.

scenario.question: Your team keeps hitting 'cannot read properties of undefined' crashes from dictionary lookups that compiled fine. What's the root cause and how do you fix it across the codebase?
scenario.directAnswer: The root cause is that, by default, index access on an index-signature/Record object returns T even when the key is missing, so the compiler lets you use a value that's actually undefined at runtime. Enable the noUncheckedIndexedAccess compiler option, which makes index access return T | undefined and forces a guard (or non-null assertion) at every dynamic lookup — converting these runtime crashes into compile errors.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A mismatch between the default index-access type (T) and runtime reality (possibly undefined).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: TypeScript's default favours ergonomics; the strict flag favours safety for dynamic keys.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: noUncheckedIndexedAccess adds | undefined to index/element access results, so reads must be narrowed before use.

scenario.whyImportant: This is the canonical index-signature pitfall and a strong signal a candidate writes robust dynamic-data code.

nestedTopics.title: Migration cost
nestedTopics.explanation: Turning the flag on surfaces many existing unsafe accesses to fix incrementally.

nestedTopics.title: Guards and assertions
nestedTopics.explanation: Use a presence check (in / === undefined) or a justified non-null assertion when you truly know the key exists.

followUps.question: Any downside to the flag?
followUps.answer: It can be noisy for known-key Record types and array loops, so teams sometimes pair it with helper functions or accept assertions where existence is guaranteed.

coding.question: Write a generic groupBy that takes an array and a key-selector, and returns a dictionary mapping each key to an array of items. Type the result with an index signature.
coding.thoughtProcess: The result is a dictionary of string keys to arrays of T, so Record<string, T[]> (an index signature). I iterate, compute each item's key via the selector, and push into the bucket — initializing the bucket if it's missing. Because index access may be undefined, I default the bucket with ?? before pushing.
coding.lineByLine: Record<string, T[]> is the index-signature result type: any string key maps to an array of items. For each item we compute its key, then out[k] ??= [] creates the bucket if it's absent before pushing. The generic T keeps the items fully typed throughout.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) — one pass over the array.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) — every item ends up in a bucket.

alternativeApproaches.title: Use a Map
alternativeApproaches.explanation: A Map<string, T[]> avoids prototype-key pitfalls and supports non-string keys.

followUps.question: Why might a Map be safer than an object dictionary here?
followUps.answer: An object inherits keys like '__proto__'/'constructor' from its prototype, which can collide with data keys; a Map has no such inherited keys and supports any key type.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Index signatures and Record type the dynamic-data layer: normalized stores (byId maps), caches, i18n dictionaries, and config bags. They give a uniform shape so utilities can operate over any dictionary generically.
productionDeepDive.performance: Types are free at runtime. The structural choice matters: plain objects are fast for small string-keyed maps, but Map outperforms and is safer for large, frequently-mutated, or non-string-keyed collections.
productionDeepDive.security: Object dictionaries inherit prototype keys (__proto__, constructor), so building one from untrusted input risks prototype pollution. Use Map or Object.create(null), and validate keys for untrusted data.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Centralize map types (Record<EntityId, Entity>) and enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess so the growing codebase handles missing keys consistently rather than crashing in new edge cases.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Choosing Record over a known key union documents exhaustiveness; an open index signature documents 'keys are data'. Either is clearer than scattering any across lookups.
productionDeepDive.observability: tsc with noUncheckedIndexedAccess turns missing-key bugs into compile errors visible in CI; without it, these only appear as runtime exceptions in logs.

caseStudies.problem: byId lookups returned undefined for ids not yet loaded, crashing selectors.
caseStudies.solution: Type byId as Record<string, Entity> and enable strict index access so selectors handle missing entities.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More null-handling boilerplate vs. crash-free selectors.
caseStudies.lessons: Strict index access plus a clear dictionary type prevents the most common normalized-state bugs.

keyTakeaways: An index signature [key: string]: T types objects with unknown keys — dictionaries, caches, and lookup tables.
Record<string, V> is essentially an index signature, but Record can also restrict keys to a known union.
You can combine named properties with an index signature, but each named value type must be assignable to it.
By default index access returns T even for missing keys; noUncheckedIndexedAccess makes it T | undefined and forces guards.
Use index signatures/Record for open-ended keys, a fixed interface for known keys, and a Map for non-string or large dynamic key sets.
